chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Sakuni al-Mazki in Kufa narrated that Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Hadrami said: Ibrahim ibn Abi Muawiyah narrated to me from his father, from al-A'mash, from Abi Zabyan, who said: Umar brought an insane woman who had committed adultery, and Umar ordered that she be stoned. They passed her by Ali (peace be upon him), and he said: 'What is this?' They said: 'An insane woman who has committed adultery, and Umar has ordered her to be stoned.' He said: 'Do not rush.' Then Umar said: 'Do you not know that the pen has been lifted from three: from the child until he matures, from the insane person until he regains consciousness, and from the sleeper until he wakes up?'

The compiler of this book, may God be pleased with him, said: This hadith came this way. The original version of this, from the words of the Ahl al-Bayt (peace be upon them), is that the insane man, if he commits adultery, is punished, but the insane woman, if she commits adultery, is not punished, because the insane man performs the act, while the insane woman is the one acted upon.

key_terms.أهل البيت: The Ahl al-Bayt (Family of the Prophet)
key_terms.رفع القلم: Lifting of the pen (exemption from accountability)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference in punishment for adultery between an insane man and an insane woman in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Khisal highlights a nuanced juristic debate regarding the hadd punishment for adultery committed by the insane, contrasting the general principle of lifting the 'pen' (accountability) with the specific Ahl al-Bayt view that distinguishes between men and women based on whether they actively commit the act or are passive recipients. It underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the distinction between temporary insanity and permanent mental incapacity in determining legal liability. The context reflects the broader Islamic legal discourse on how mental state interacts with the physical act of zina.
